title: Ventriculostomy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Ventriculostomy is a common and life-saving neurosurgical procedure used to manage acute hydrocephalus, monitor intracranial pressure, and treat complications such as shunt infections or obstructions. The technique involves placing a catheter into the cerebral ventricles to drain cerebrospinal fluid, relieving elevated intracranial pressure and preventing further neurologic compromise. Advances in image-guided and neuronavigation-assisted techniques have improved accuracy and safety, yet ventriculostomy remains associated with significant risks, including ventriculitis, hemorrhage, malposition, obstruction, and overdrainage. Clinical success depends on precise catheter placement, adherence to aseptic technique, and vigilant postoperative monitoring. Despite procedural standardization, outcome variability persists due to inconsistent protocol adherence, inadequate infection prevention measures, and differences in interprofessional communication. Effective management requires a multidisciplinary approach involving neurosurgeons, critical care clinicians, nurses, and infection prevention specialists to ensure patient safety and optimize neurological recovery.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course teaches clinicians comprehensive knowledge of ventriculostomy indications, contraindications, procedural techniques, and evidence-based management strategies. Learners develop competence in selecting appropriate entry sites, applying neuronavigation tools, and implementing standardized care bundles to reduce complications. Emphasis is placed on sterile technique, consistent intracranial pressure monitoring, and prompt recognition of catheter-related issues. The course reinforces the value of interprofessional collaboration, as coordinated efforts among neurosurgery, nursing, infectious disease, and critical care teams enhance early detection of complications, improve communication, and support timely interventions. By integrating evidence-based protocols and collaborative care practices, clinicians strengthen procedural safety, reduce morbidity, and advance neurologic outcomes for patients requiring ventriculostomy.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Introduction
content: Ventriculostomy is one of the most common emergency neurosurgical procedures performed worldwide. [1] Approximately 20,000 patients undergo ventriculostomy annually in the United States alone. [2] Claude-Nicholas Le Cat is credited with performing the first successful ventricular puncture, although his initial attempts were unsuccessful. In the 1700s, Robert Whytt and Benjamin Hill believed the procedure would hasten death, so they considered it a last resort. [3] In 1941, Ingraham and Campbell were successful in performing the procedure using the following innovations: A closed drainage system A stopcock to prevent overdrainage A drip chamber to prevent backflow of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) A flexible silicone tube for subcutaneous tunneling

title: Ventriculostomy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Herophilus and Erasistratus were the first to anatomically describe the brain's ventricular system. Later, Domenico Felice Antonio Cotugno described the presence of CSF within this interconnecting system. The ventricular system develops from cavities within the embryonic brain vesicles. The cavity of the rhombencephalon forms the fourth ventricle, the cavity of the diencephalon forms the third ventricle, and the telencephalon develops into the lateral ventricles. The cavity of the mesencephalon forms the cerebral aqueduct, which connects the third and fourth ventricles. [4]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Indications
content: Indications for performing ventriculostomy include the following: Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus: Most commonly following subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke, or meningitis. Intracranial pressure monitoring: A flexible external ventricular drain protocol is associated with improved outcomes among patients with severe traumatic brain injury. Infected ventriculoperitoneal shunts: Adjunct management for malfunctioning shunts. Intraoperative brain edema Therapeutic interventions: Administration of  thrombolytics, antibiotics, or vasodilators. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, "Nimodipine," for further information. [5] [6] [7] [8]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Contraindications
content: The contraindications for ventriculostomy include: Concurrent anticoagulant therapy Coagulopathy Scalp infection Intracranial abscess. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Intracranial Pressure Monitoring, " for further information.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Equipment
content: Basic equipment sets for ventriculostomy include the following: Preparation: Nonsterile gloves, soap, brush, hand towel, razor, and a marker pen for placement of monitoring devices. Procedure: A face mask, sterile gown and gloves, antiseptic solution, drape, local anesthetic agent, 5-mL syringe, 11- or 15-gauge surgical blade, ventricular catheter, and ICP-monitoring kit. Depending on the technique, a drill with a drill bit, a bolt, an ICP sensor, and a transducer may be required. Suture material and sterile dressing are also needed. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Intracranial Pressure Monitoring, " for further information.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Preparation
content: Patients and caregivers should receive a detailed explanation of the procedure and its associated risks, and written informed consent should be obtained before the procedure. Strict adherence to aseptic guidelines is a cornerstone of preventing infection. Prophylactic antibiotics should be administered at the initiation of the procedure. [9] A meticulous technique is pivotal in minimizing procedure-related complications. Patients should be adequately sedated, have a secured airway, and receive a local anesthetic at the designated ventriculostomy site.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Technique or Treatment
content: Kocher point: 1 to 2 cm anterior to the coronal suture in the midpupillary line, or 11 cm posterior to the glabella and 3 to 4 cm lateral to the midline, ipsilateral to the medial canthus, along a line extending coronally from the ipsilateral tragus In freehand ventriculostomy from this point, the contralateral medial canthus and the region perpendicular to the skull are more reliable surface landmarks for accurate ventriculostomy than the ipsilateral medial canthus. Kocher point is the preferred location for ventriculostomy. [11]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Technique or Treatment
content: Ghajar first introduced a ventricular catheter guide to optimize the trajectory during ventriculostomy. He advocated a perpendicular trajectory relative to the surface of the skull. [12] However, the calvarial slope often limits this trajectory, especially in the coronal plane. [13] [14] The accuracy of the ideal placement of the ventricular tip is approximately 86%. Furthermore, 3.1% of the catheters are nonfunctional and require replacement or repositioning. [15] The accuracy improves with ultrasonography, endoscopy, neuronavigation, and the adjustable Ghajar guide technique. [13] [14] Kakarla Grading of Catheter Placement: Grade 1 (optimal): Ipsilateral frontal horn, including the tip of the third ventricle Grade 2 (suboptimal, noneloquent area): Contralateral frontal horn, corpus callosum, or interhemispheric fissure Grade 3 (suboptimal, eloquent area): Basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus, brainstem, cerebellum, basal cisterns, and occipital cortex [16]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Complications
content: Results from a study evaluated outcomes among patients with primary and secondary intraventricular hemorrhages showed that approximately 40% developed complications and 35% required permanent CSF diversion procedures. [21] Factors that increase the risk of infection include: CSF leak System obstruction Frequent CSF sampling (each sampling increases the risk by 8.3%) Increased duration of catheter placement (9.3% with ≥8 days) Frequent catheter changes (each change increases risk 4-fold) Catheter irrigation [2] [22] [23] [24] [25]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Complications
content: Skin microbiota and biofilm play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of infection. However, a consensus definition of ventriculostomy-related infections (VRI) has not been established. Although the incidence of VRI can be as high as 35%, as many as 25% of patients receive unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics. [26] Notably, the cumulative rates for definitive VRI are nearly half those of suspected VRI (8.4% vs 13.5%). [27] No single intervention successfully prevents infection; however, limiting the duration of ventricular catheterization is the most effective. [28]

content: Furthermore, a stewardship and ventriculostomy-related infection score may guide antibiotic decision-making. [29] No significant differences in infection risk or complication have been observed between EVDs placed in the operating room versus at the bedside. The surgeons' experience also did not influence the outcome. [1] [30] An absolute risk reduction of approximately 20% has been reported when an antibiotic-coated catheter is used. [2] The anatomical point of ventriculostomy has not been shown to affect the risk of infection. [2] However, strict adherence to EVD care bundles is crucial in reducing the risk of infection. The best strategy is to avoid insertion unless necessary. [22]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Complications
content: The misplacement rate of the EVD ranges from 12.3% to 60%. [16] [31] Results from a systematic review found the ipsilateral medial epicanthus as the favored anatomical trajectory for frontal ventriculostomy. Kakarla grade 1 placement was achieved in 68.58% of procedures, while Kakarla grade 3 placement occurred in 10.21% of cases. [32] Suboptimal placements were associated with longer intracranial catheter length. [33] Using navigation and augmented reality improves the accurate placement of EVDs. [34] [35] [36] [37] Using bolt EVDs has minimal risk of CSF leak and tube migration. [3] Rapid weaning within 24 hours is recommended over gradual elevation and clamping of the drain. [22]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Clinical Significance
content: Ventricular catheters provide global ICP monitoring with minimal drift and influence from pressure gradients between the parenchyma and ventricular system. EVPs are the most reliable method for achieving maximum accuracy at minimal expense. Additional therapeutic benefits of CSF drainage include the instillation of medications such as antibiotics and thrombolytic agents. The advantage of the ventricular monitoring device is its ability to facilitate the egress of CSF during a sustained rise in ICP (≥20 mm Hg for ≥5 minutes). However, the disadvantage is that simultaneous monitoring and CSF drainage are impossible. The recommended target ICP (10 mm Hg) or ICP waveform analysis guides the amount of CSF drained. This value is obtained from the concurrent application of intraparenchymal monitors or clinical neurological examination. Paradoxical upward transtentorial herniation is prevented by avoiding excessive drainage of CSF.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Clinical Significance
content: An EVD can be removed once ICP normalizes and the motor score is at least 5 for 48 to 72 hours without any interventions such as clamping or gradual height increases (training of the EVD). [38] Strict aseptic precautions must be implemented during removal. The head should be lowered to prevent the risk of pneumocephalus and pneumoventriculi. If a fever with meningitis-like symptoms persists, the catheter tip may be sent for bacteriological analysis. The wound is closed in layers to minimize the CSF leak and infection risk. Patients require close monitoring for any signs of clinical deterioration for at least 24 hours after removal, with preparations in place for the emergency reinsertion. [38] Substantial gaps in adherence to EVD care guidelines include: EVD clamp trials (81% adherence) Indication-based CSF sampling (67% adherence) Tunneling catheter placement (40% adherence) [39] Therefore, the implementation of quality improvement initiatives is significant.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Monitoring ICP requires an interprofessional team approach involving clinicians, specialists, and specialty-trained nurses collaborating across disciplines to achieve optimal patient outcomes. Surgically trained nurses are crucial in assisting and monitoring the surgeon intraoperatively. Deviation from these standards can result in life-threatening complications. Open communication among team members ensures optimal outcomes and patient safety.

title: Ventriculostomy -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Members of the interprofessional healthcare team assist in the following: Drawing CSF for culture Assisting the surgeon with medication administration Monitoring for signs of intracranial hypertension Checking for CSF leak Ensuring aseptic technique when manipulating the catheter Monitoring the ICP tracing for dampening or lack of pulsation

title: Ventriculostomy -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring
content: Nurses involved in patient care should monitor the following: Hourly CSF drainage Oscillation of CSF within the tubes Absence of wound seepage Correct height of the EVD Zeroing of the EVD height at the level of the foramen of Monro or tragus of the ear Frequent neurological assessments [8]

title: Ventriculostomy -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring
content: Strict adherence to recommended checklists is required. [8] Maintaining a sterile environment and implementing stringent monitoring to anticipate and promptly address complications are the cornerstones of the care bundle approach. [43]
